## Understanding Supercomputing Demand and Project Objectives

::: {style="margin-top: 30px;"}

<div style="background-color: #EAF3F9; border-left: 5px solid #006DAE; padding: 4px 12px; margin: 0 0 10px 0; color: #005B91; font-weight: bold; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.1;">
What is Supercomputing (HPC)?
</div>

High-performance computing (HPC) uses **thousands of processors working together** to solve complex problems.

**How does it work?** CPUs handle general computing tasks, while GPUs accelerate highly parallel calculations.

**Research applications:** Drug discovery, climate modelling, weather forecasting, and engineering simulations.

<div style="height: 10px;"></div>

<div style="background-color: #EAF3F9; border-left: 5px solid #006DAE; padding: 4px 12px; margin: 12px 0 10px 0; color: #005B91; font-weight: bold; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.1;">
Understanding Computing Resources Term
</div>

- [**Demand (Requested)**]{style="color: #006DAE;"}: Computing resources researchers **request**.
- [**Allocation**]{style="color: #006DAE;"}: Computing resources **awarded** to researchers.
- [**Unmet demand**]{style="color: #006DAE;"}: Requests **not fulfilled**, when the measures are comparable.

:::

<div style="height: 10px;"></div>

<div style="background-color: #EAF3F9; border-left: 5px solid #006DAE; padding: 4px 12px; margin: 12px 0 10px 0; color: #005B91; font-weight: bold; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.1;">
Project Objective
</div>

To develop **demand projections and alternative scenarios through 2030** for Australia's national research supercomputing infrastructure, helping inform future HPC planning under uncertainty.

::: {style="font-size: 0.48em; color: #666; margin-top: 8px;"}

Source: [@ibm_hpc; @NCMAS2026]

:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Load harmonised historical dataset
annual_converted <- readRDS(
  "../assets/data/data converted/annual_demand_allocation_converted.rds"
)

# Load original GPU historical scenarios
historical_gpu_scenarios <- readRDS(
  "../assets/data/data converted/historical_gpu_scenarios.rds"
)

# Verify scenario coverage
stopifnot(
  nrow(historical_gpu_scenarios) == 8,
  identical(
    sort(as.integer(historical_gpu_scenarios$year)),
    2014:2021
  )
)

# Prepare historical series
historical_plot <- annual_converted |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),

    `Overall HPC|Demand` = demand_ksu / 1e6,
    `Overall HPC|Allocation` = allocation_ksu / 1e6,

    `CPU|Demand` = demand_cpu_core_hours / 1e6,
    `CPU|Allocation` = allocation_cpu_core_hours / 1e6,

    `GPU|Demand` = demand_gpu_hours / 1e6,
    `GPU|Allocation` = allocation_gpu_hours / 1e6
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -year,
    names_to = c("resource", "measure"),
    names_sep = "\\|",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  mutate(
    resource = factor(
      resource,
      levels = c("Overall HPC", "CPU", "GPU"),
      labels = c(
        "Overall HPC (million kSU)",
        "CPU (million core-hours)",
        "GPU (million GPU-hours)"
      )
    ),
    measure = factor(
      measure,
      levels = c("Demand", "Allocation")
    )
  )

# Prepare GPU low/high scenario bands, 2014–2021
gpu_uncertainty_data <- historical_gpu_scenarios |>
  select(
    year,
    demand_gpu_hours_low,
    demand_gpu_hours_high,
    allocation_gpu_hours_low,
    allocation_gpu_hours_high
  ) |>
  filter(
    year >= 2014,
    year <= 2021
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -year,
    names_to = c("measure", ".value"),
    names_pattern =
      "(demand|allocation)_(gpu_hours_low|gpu_hours_high)"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      demand = "Demand",
      allocation = "Allocation"
    ),
    measure = factor(
      measure,
      levels = c("Demand", "Allocation")
    ),
    resource = factor(
      "GPU (million GPU-hours)",
      levels = levels(historical_plot$resource)
    ),
    gpu_hours_low = gpu_hours_low / 1e6,
    gpu_hours_high = gpu_hours_high / 1e6
  )

# Create historical demand and allocation chart
ggplot() +

  # GPU scenario bands, 2014–2021
  geom_ribbon(
    data = gpu_uncertainty_data,
    aes(
      x = year,
      ymin = gpu_hours_low,
      ymax = gpu_hours_high,
      fill = measure,
      group = measure
    ),
    alpha = 0.18,
    colour = NA
  ) +

  # Solid lines:
  # All HPC and CPU years, plus GPU 2022–2026
  geom_line(
    data = historical_plot |>
      filter(
        resource != "GPU (million GPU-hours)" |
          year >= 2022
      ),
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = value,
      colour = measure,
      group = interaction(resource, measure)
    ),
    linewidth = 1.15
  ) +

  # Dashed GPU scenarios, 2014–2021
  geom_line(
    data = historical_plot |>
      filter(
        resource == "GPU (million GPU-hours)",
        year <= 2021
      ),
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = value,
      colour = measure,
      group = measure
    ),
    linewidth = 1.15,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +

  # Connect scenario period to 2022
  geom_line(
    data = historical_plot |>
      filter(
        resource == "GPU (million GPU-hours)",
        year %in% c(2021, 2022)
      ),
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = value,
      group = measure
    ),
    colour = "#999999",
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "dotted"
  ) +

  # Demand and allocation observations
  geom_point(
    data = historical_plot,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = value,
      colour = measure
    ),
    size = 1.8
  ) +

  # GPU scenario / usable-data boundary
  geom_vline(
    data = data.frame(
      resource = factor(
        "GPU (million GPU-hours)",
        levels = levels(historical_plot$resource)
      ),
      boundary = 2021.5
    ),
    aes(xintercept = boundary),
    linetype = "dotted",
    colour = "#888888",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +

  # Resource panels
  facet_wrap(
    ~resource,
    nrow = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +

  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Demand" = "#006DAE",
      "Allocation" = "#E69F00"
    )
  ) +

  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Demand" = "#006DAE",
      "Allocation" = "#E69F00"
    )
  ) +

  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(2014, 2017, 2020, 2023, 2026)
  ) +

  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1),
    limits = c(0, NA),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +

  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = NULL,
    colour = NULL,
    fill = NULL
  ) +

  guides(fill = "none") +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +

  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(
      size = 14,
      face = "bold",
      colour = "#17324D"
    ),
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#EAF2F9",
      colour = NA
    ),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1,
      size = 10
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.3, "cm"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(1, "lines"),
    plot.margin = margin(5, 8, 2, 8)
  )
```

<p>
<span class="period">2023 - 2026:</span>
Official Setonix GPU requests
increased <strong>123%</strong>

</p>

<strong>GPU demand is growing,</strong>
but historical GPU-hour estimates

</p>

</div>

</div>

<div class="slide7-note">
<strong>Interpretation:</strong>
Historical series include reported and estimated values.
GPU values before 2022 are assumption-based historical scenarios,
not observed demand or statistical confidence intervals.
System transitions may affect comparability but are not confirmed
causes of demand changes.
The 2025 HPC estimate affects reconstructed 2026 growth.
The 2026 HPC allocation excludes 12,000 kSU for Setonix Q.
Panel units and scales differ.
</div>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(stringr)

# Load historical FoR data
for_converted <- readRDS(
  "../assets/data/data converted/field_of_research_converted.rds"
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(for_converted) == 133,
  identical(
    sort(unique(as.integer(for_converted$year))),
    2014:2026
  )
)

# Consistent colours
for_palette <- c(
  "Physical Sciences" = "#006DAE",
  "Chemical Sciences" = "#38A6D8",
  "Earth & Environmental Sciences" = "#279A8B",
  "Engineering & Technology" = "#E69F00",
  "Biological & Agricultural Sciences" = "#74B86A",
  "Medical & Health Sciences" = "#B77DBD",
  "Mathematics & Computing" = "#E27B66",
  "Social Sciences, Humanities & Built Environment" = "#8B91A9",
  "Unclassified & Operational" = "#B7BEC7"
)

field_order <- names(for_palette)

# ----------------------------------------
# Overall: harmonised groups, 2014–2026
# ----------------------------------------

for_overall <- for_converted |>
  mutate(
    reported_clean = research_field_reported |>
      str_remove("^\\s*\\d{2}\\s+") |>
      str_to_lower() |>
      str_replace_all("&", " and ") |>
      str_squish(),

    field = case_when(
      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "physical sciences|radioastronomy|radio astronomy"
      ) ~ "Physical Sciences",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "chemical sciences"
      ) ~ "Chemical Sciences",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "earth|environmental|geoscien"
      ) ~ "Earth & Environmental Sciences",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "engineering|technology"
      ) ~ "Engineering & Technology",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "biological|agricultural|veterinary|food sciences"
      ) ~ "Biological & Agricultural Sciences",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "medical|health|biomedical|clinical"
      ) ~ "Medical & Health Sciences",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "mathematical|computing|information"
      ) ~ "Mathematics & Computing",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        paste0(
          "psychology|economics|history|archaeology|",
          "human society|language|communication|culture|",
          "philosophy|religious|built environment|design"
        )
      ) ~ "Social Sciences, Humanities & Built Environment",

      str_detect(
        reported_clean,
        "other|unreported|unclassified|pawsey operations"
      ) ~ "Unclassified & Operational",

      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(for_overall$field),
  n_distinct(for_overall$field) == 9
)

for_overall_plot <- for_overall |>
  group_by(year, field) |>
  summarise(
    allocation_share = sum(allocation_share_for),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ----------------------------------------
# Early period: FoR 2008, 2014–2020
# ----------------------------------------

for_early <- for_converted |>
  filter(between(year, 2014, 2020)) |>
  mutate(
    field = case_when(
      for_2008_division_code == "01" ~
        "Mathematics & Computing",

      for_2008_division_code == "02" ~
        "Physical Sciences",

      for_2008_division_code == "03" ~
        "Chemical Sciences",

      for_2008_division_code %in% c(
        "04", "05", "04 + 05"
      ) ~ "Earth & Environmental Sciences",

      for_2008_division_code %in% c(
        "06", "07"
      ) ~ "Biological & Agricultural Sciences",

      for_2008_division_code == "08" ~
        "Mathematics & Computing",

      for_2008_division_code %in% c(
        "09", "10", "09 + 10"
      ) ~ "Engineering & Technology",

      for_2008_division_code == "11" ~
        "Medical & Health Sciences",

      for_2008_division_code %in% c(
        "12", "21"
      ) ~ "Social Sciences, Humanities & Built Environment",

      is.na(for_2008_division_code) ~
        "Unclassified & Operational",

      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

stopifnot(!anyNA(for_early$field))

for_early_plot <- for_early |>
  group_by(year, field) |>
  summarise(
    allocation_share = sum(allocation_share_for),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ----------------------------------------
# Later period: FoR 2020, 2021–2026
# ----------------------------------------

for_late <- for_converted |>
  filter(between(year, 2021, 2026)) |>
  mutate(
    field = case_when(
      for_standard_2020 %in% c(
        "Engineering",
        "Engineering + Technology",
        "Technology — no direct FoR 2020 alignment"
      ) ~ "Engineering & Technology",

      for_standard_2020 == "Physical sciences" ~
        "Physical Sciences",

      for_standard_2020 == "Chemical sciences" ~
        "Chemical Sciences",

      for_standard_2020 %in% c(
        "Earth sciences",
        "Environmental sciences",
        "Earth sciences + Environmental sciences"
      ) ~ "Earth & Environmental Sciences",

      for_standard_2020 %in% c(
        "Biological sciences",
        "Agricultural, veterinary and food sciences"
      ) ~ "Biological & Agricultural Sciences",

      for_standard_2020 %in% c(
        "Biomedical and clinical sciences",
        "Health sciences",
        "Biomedical and clinical sciences + Health sciences"
      ) ~ "Medical & Health Sciences",

      for_standard_2020 %in% c(
        "Mathematical sciences",
        "Information and computing sciences"
      ) ~ "Mathematics & Computing",

      for_standard_2020 %in% c(
        "Psychology",
        "Economics",
        "History, heritage and archaeology",
        "Language, communication and culture",
        "Philosophy and religious studies",
        "Human society",
        "Built environment and design"
      ) ~ "Social Sciences, Humanities & Built Environment",

      for_standard_2020 == "Other / Unclassified" ~
        "Unclassified & Operational",

      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

stopifnot(!anyNA(for_late$field))

for_late_plot <- for_late |>
  group_by(year, field) |>
  summarise(
    allocation_share = sum(allocation_share_for),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Validate annual shares before plotting
for (dataset in list(
  for_overall_plot,
  for_early_plot,
  for_late_plot
)) {
  totals <- dataset |>
    group_by(year) |>
    summarise(
      total = sum(allocation_share),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  stopifnot(
    all(abs(totals$total - 1) < 1e-6)
  )
}

# Include absent categories as zero
prepare_for <- function(data) {
  data |>
    mutate(
      field = factor(field, levels = field_order)
    ) |>
    complete(
      year,
      field,
      fill = list(allocation_share = 0)
    )
}

for_overall_plot <- prepare_for(for_overall_plot)
for_early_plot <- prepare_for(for_early_plot)
for_late_plot <- prepare_for(for_late_plot)

# Average annual allocation shares
for_early_average <- for_early_plot |>
  group_by(field) |>
  summarise(
    mean_share = mean(allocation_share),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

for_late_average <- for_late_plot |>
  group_by(field) |>
  summarise(
    mean_share = mean(allocation_share),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Annual leading field
for_top_overall <- for_overall_plot |>
  arrange(year, field) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    ymid = cumsum(allocation_share) -
      allocation_share / 2
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    allocation_share,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    label = percent(
      allocation_share,
      accuracy = 1
    )
  )

# Short labels for average-share charts
short_field_labels <- c(
  "Physical Sciences" = "Physical Sciences",
  "Chemical Sciences" = "Chemical Sciences",
  "Earth & Environmental Sciences" = "Earth & Environmental",
  "Engineering & Technology" = "Engineering & Technology",
  "Biological & Agricultural Sciences" = "Biological & Agricultural",
  "Medical & Health Sciences" = "Medical & Health",
  "Mathematics & Computing" = "Mathematics & Computing",
  "Social Sciences, Humanities & Built Environment" =
    "Social Sciences & Humanities",
  "Unclassified & Operational" =
    "Unclassified & Operational"
)

# ----------------------------------------
# Annual composition chart
# ----------------------------------------

plot_for_overall <- function(data) {
  ggplot(
    data,
    aes(
      x = factor(year),
      y = allocation_share,
      fill = field
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(
      width = 0.83,
      position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)
    ) +
    geom_text(
      data = for_top_overall,
      aes(
        x = factor(year),
        y = ymid,
        label = label
      ),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      colour = "white",
      fontface = "bold",
      size = 3
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = for_palette,
      limits = field_order,
      drop = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      labels = label_percent(),
      breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = NULL,
      fill = NULL
    ) +
    guides(
      fill = guide_legend(
        ncol = 3,
        byrow = TRUE
      )
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
      legend.key.size = grid::unit(0.3, "cm"),
      legend.spacing.y = grid::unit(0.05, "cm"),
      plot.margin = margin(3, 6, 2, 6)
    )
}

# ----------------------------------------
# Period-average charts
# ----------------------------------------

plot_for_average <- function(data) {
  chart_data <- data |>
    arrange(mean_share) |>
    mutate(
      field_label = unname(
        short_field_labels[as.character(field)]
      ),
      field_label = factor(
        field_label,
        levels = field_label
      )
    )

  ggplot(
    chart_data,
    aes(
      x = mean_share,
      y = field_label,
      fill = field
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(width = 0.68) +
    geom_text(
      aes(
        label = percent(
          mean_share,
          accuracy = 1
        )
      ),
      hjust = -0.15,
      size = 2.8,
      colour = "#17324D",
      fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = for_palette,
      guide = "none"
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      labels = label_percent(),
      breaks = seq(0, 0.5, 0.1),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.margin = margin(3, 12, 2, 3)
    )
}
```

<div class="slide8-insights">

<div class="slide8-insight">

<div class="slide8-insight-title">
2014–2020 | Earth & Environmental
</div>

<p>
<strong>32% average share.</strong>
Climate, weather and geoscience are
established national HPC workloads.
This provides context for the field's
historical concentration, but does not
identify the projects driving each year.
</p>

</div>

<div class="slide8-insight">

<div class="slide8-insight-title">
2021–2026 | Engineering
</div>

<p>
<strong>35% average share;</strong>
a peak of <strong>41% in 2022</strong>.
NCMAS documents large computational
engineering projects, including turbine
and fluid-flow simulations.
Their contribution to annual shares
requires project-level verification.
</p>

</div>

<div class="slide8-insight">

<div class="slide8-insight-title">
Why the apparent shift needs caution
</div>

<p>
The comparison crosses
<strong>FoR 2008 and FoR 2020</strong>
classifications. Category changes,
harmonisation choices and the
different 2017 Pawsey reporting scope
limit direct interpretation as a change
in research priorities.
</p>

</div>

</div>

::: {.slide8-note}
**Note:** Shares represent allocations, not demand. FoR 2008/2020 classification changes and differences in reporting coverage limit direct comparisons across years.

<div class="slide9">

<div class="slide9-intro">
<strong>Why simple models?</strong>
I have <strong>13 years of HPC and CPU data (2014 - 2026)</strong>
and only <strong>5 years of GPU data (2022 - 2026)</strong>.
I compared four simple forecasting models.
</div>

<div class="slide9-models">

<div class="slide9-model">

<div class="slide9-model-title">
Naïve | No growth
</div>

<div class="slide9-equation">
$\hat{D}_{T+h}=D_T$
</div>

<div class="slide9-model-desc">
Future demand stays at the <strong>latest level</strong>.
</div>

</div>

<div class="slide9-model">

<div class="slide9-model-title">
Drift | Average growth
</div>

<div class="slide9-equation">
$\hat{D}_{T+h}=D_T+h\frac{D_T-D_1}{T-1}$
</div>

<div class="slide9-model-desc">
Extends the <strong>average yearly change</strong>.
</div>

</div>

<div class="slide9-model">

<div class="slide9-model-title">
Linear | Fixed annual growth
</div>

<div class="slide9-equation">
$D_t=\alpha+\beta t+\varepsilon_t$
</div>

<div class="slide9-model-desc">
Assumes a <strong>constant yearly change</strong>.
</div>

</div>

<div class="slide9-model">

<div class="slide9-model-title">
Log-linear | Percentage growth
</div>

<div class="slide9-equation">
$\log(D_t)=\alpha+\beta t+\varepsilon_t$
</div>

<div class="slide9-model-desc">
Assumes a <strong>constant percentage growth rate</strong>.
</div>

</div>

</div>

<div class="slide9-section">
Sensitivity Analysis | How much does 2026 affect the trend?
</div>

<div class="slide9-reason">
I fitted the <strong>linear model twice</strong>:
first without 2026, then with 2026.
I compared the estimated annual growth.
</div>

<table class="slide9-results">

<thead>
<tr>
<th>Resource</th>
<th>Without 2026</th>
<th>With 2026</th>
<th>Change</th>
</tr>
</thead>

<tbody>

<tr>
<td>Overall HPC</td>
<td>144,357 kSU/year</td>
<td class="slide9-highlight">161,992 kSU/year</td>
<td class="slide9-highlight">+12.2%</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CPU</td>
<td>72.41M core-hours/year</td>
<td class="slide9-highlight">81.01M core-hours/year</td>
<td class="slide9-highlight">+11.9%</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>GPU</td>
<td>0.012M GPU-hours/year</td>
<td class="slide9-highlight">0.172M GPU-hours/year</td>
<td>Highly sensitive</td>
</tr>

</tbody>

</table>

<div class="slide9-finding">
<strong>Key finding:</strong>
Including 2026 increases the estimated annual growth
by around <strong>12% for HPC and CPU</strong>.
GPU results are much more sensitive because only
<strong>five years of data</strong> are available.
</div>

<div class="slide9-for">
<strong>Fields of Research (FoR):</strong>
I first forecast <strong>total HPC demand for 2030</strong>,
then apply the <strong>average allocation shares from 2021 - 2026</strong>
to create scenarios for each research field.
These are <strong>allocation-share-based scenarios</strong>,
not separate forecasts of FoR demand.
</div>

<div class="slide9-note">
<strong>Note:</strong>
GPU models use only 2022 - 2026 data.
Sensitivity shows changes in fitted growth rates,
not forecast accuracy.
</div>

</div>

::: {style="font-size: 10px; color: #666; margin-top: 4px; line-height: 1.15;"}

**Methods:** Naïve, drift, linear and log-linear models
[@HyndmanAthanasopoulos2021].
Sensitivity results: project calculations.

:::

::: {.slide10}

::: {.slide10-intro}

**How did I compare the models?**
I tested how well each model predicted the next year using historical data.

:::

::: {.slide10-method}

**Method:** Expanding-window, one-step-ahead cross-validation.
Train on earlier years, predict the next year, then repeat with more data.

**Accuracy:** RMSE measures forecast errors and gives more weight to large mistakes. MAE measures average absolute error. **Lower is better.**

:::

::: {.slide10-chart}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 3.45
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

accuracy_data <- data.frame(
  resource = rep(
    c("Overall HPC", "CPU", "GPU"),
    each = 4
  ),
  model = rep(
    c("Naïve", "Drift", "Linear", "Log-linear"),
    times = 3
  ),
  RMSE = c(
    378864, 314588, 290898, 511614,
    260.05, 242.61, 157.72, 160.18,
    0.441, 0.537, 0.729, 0.719
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    resource = factor(
      resource,
      levels = c("Overall HPC", "CPU", "GPU"),
      labels = c(
        "Overall HPC (thousand kSU)",
        "CPU (million core-hours)",
        "GPU (million GPU-hours)"
      )
    ),
    model = factor(
      model,
      levels = c("Naïve", "Drift", "Linear", "Log-linear")
    ),
    plot_rmse = if_else(
      resource == "Overall HPC (thousand kSU)",
      RMSE / 1000,
      RMSE
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(resource) |>
  mutate(
    best = plot_rmse == min(plot_rmse),
    label = if_else(
      resource == "Overall HPC (thousand kSU)",
      sprintf("%.1f", plot_rmse),
      sprintf("%.2f", plot_rmse)
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(
  accuracy_data,
  aes(x = model, y = plot_rmse, fill = best)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    vjust = -0.45,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    colour = "#17324D"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ resource,
    nrow = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "#006DAE",
      "FALSE" = "#A9CDE3"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, NA),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.17))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Cross-validation RMSE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(
      size = 13,
      face = "bold",
      colour = "#17324D"
    ),
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#EAF3F9",
      colour = NA
    ),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      size = 10,
      angle = 30,
      hjust = 1
    ),
```

## Model Diagnostics: Checking the Linear Models

<style>
.slide11 {
  width: 100%;
  margin-top: 4px;
  font-size: 15px;
  line-height: 1.23;
}

.slide11-intro {
  font-size: 16px;
  line-height: 1.3;
  margin-bottom: 10px;
}

.slide11-heading {
  color: #17324D;
  font-size: 19px;
  font-weight: 700;
  margin: 10px 0 7px;
}

.slide11-chart {
  width: 100%;
  margin-top: 3px;
}

.slide11-chart .cell,
.slide11-chart .cell-output,
.slide11-chart .cell-output-display {
  width: 100% !important;
  max-width: 100% !important;
}

.slide11-chart img {
  display: block;
  width: 100% !important;
  height: auto;
  margin: 0 auto;
}

.slide11-diagnostics {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
  gap: 14px;
  margin-top: 8px;
}

.slide11-diagnostic {
  background: #F2F7FB;
  border-left: 4px solid #006DAE;
  padding: 10px 13px;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 1.3;
}

.slide11-diagnostic strong {
  color: #17324D;
}

.slide11-diagnostic p {
  margin: 5px 0;
}

.slide11-caution {
  background: #F2F7FB;
  border-left: 5px solid #006DAE;
  margin-top: 13px;
  padding: 11px 14px;
  font-size: 15px;
  line-height: 1.3;
}

.slide11-note {
  margin-top: 9px;
  font-size: 10px;
  line-height: 1.2;
  color: #555;
}
</style>

::: {.slide11}

::: {.slide11-intro}
**What did I check?** After selecting linear models for **overall HPC and CPU**, I examined their residuals using **Q–Q plots** and **Ljung–Box tests**.

Q–Q plots check whether residuals are approximately normally distributed. Ljung–Box tests check whether residuals are correlated across years.
:::

::: {.slide11-heading}
Residual Diagnostics: Overall HPC and CPU
:::

::: {.slide11-chart}

```{r}
#| label: slide11-residual-diagnostics
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Locate the repository root reproducibly
# -------------------------------------------------------

# The here package uses project-root markers such as
# an .Rproj file, .here file, or Git repository.

if (!requireNamespace("here", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop(
    "The 'here' package is required. ",
    "Install it with install.packages('here')."
  )
}

project_root <- here::here()

hpc_path <- here::here(
  "assets",
  "models",
  "overall_hpc_models.rds"
)

cpu_path <- here::here(
  "assets",
  "models",
  "cpu_models.rds"
)

# Check that here() has identified the correct project.
if (!file.exists(hpc_path) || !file.exists(cpu_path)) {
  stop(
    "Saved model files were not found.\n",
    "Project root detected: ", project_root, "\n",
    "Expected HPC file: ", hpc_path, "\n",
    "Expected CPU file: ", cpu_path, "\n",
    "Check the project root and assets/models folder."
  )
}

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Load the original fitted forecasting models
# -------------------------------------------------------

hpc_models <- readRDS(hpc_path)
cpu_models <- readRDS(cpu_path)

overall_linear <- hpc_models$overall_linear
cpu_linear <- cpu_models$cpu_linear

if (!inherits(overall_linear, "lm") ||
    !inherits(cpu_linear, "lm")) {
  stop(
    "The saved files must contain the fitted ",
    "overall_linear and cpu_linear lm objects."
  )
}

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Extract residuals
# -------------------------------------------------------

hpc_residuals <- as.numeric(
  residuals(overall_linear)
)

cpu_residuals <- as.numeric(
  residuals(cpu_linear)
)

stopifnot(
  length(hpc_residuals) >= 3,
  length(cpu_residuals) >= 3,
  all(is.finite(hpc_residuals)),
  all(is.finite(cpu_residuals))
)

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Recalculate Ljung-Box tests
# -------------------------------------------------------

# Match the diagnostic specification in the report:
# lag = 2, fitdf = 0.

hpc_lb <- Box.test(
  hpc_residuals,
  lag = 2,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

cpu_lb <- Box.test(
  cpu_residuals,
  lag = 2,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

# Check consistency with the previously reported values.
if (
  abs(hpc_lb$p.value - 0.8775) > 0.001 ||
  abs(cpu_lb$p.value - 0.3608) > 0.001
) {
  stop(
    "Ljung-Box p-values differ from the original report. ",
    "Check the saved model versions and test settings."
  )
}

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Prepare data for Q-Q plots
# -------------------------------------------------------

qq_data <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    Resource = "Overall HPC",
    Residual = hpc_residuals
  ),
  data.frame(
    Resource = "CPU",
    Residual = cpu_residuals
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    Resource = factor(
      Resource,
      levels = c("Overall HPC", "CPU")
    )
  )

# -------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Draw the two Q-Q plots
# -------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  qq_data,
  aes(sample = Residual)
) +
  stat_qq(
    colour = "#17324D",
    size = 2.0
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    colour = "#006DAE",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Resource,
    nrow = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Theoretical normal quantiles",
    y = "Sample residual quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(
      size = 13,
      face = "bold",
      colour = "#17324D"
    ),
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#EAF3F9",
      colour = NA
    ),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.5, "lines"),
    plot.margin = margin(5, 10, 5, 5)
  )
```

:::

<div class="slide11-diagnostics">

<div class="slide11-diagnostic">
<strong>Overall HPC</strong>
<p>Ljung–Box test (lag 2): <strong>p = `r sprintf("%.4f", hpc_lb$p.value)`</strong></p>
<p>No significant autocorrelation detected. The Q–Q plot shows some departures from normality.</p>
</div>

<div class="slide11-diagnostic">
<strong>CPU</strong>
<p>Ljung–Box test (lag 2): <strong>p = `r sprintf("%.4f", cpu_lb$p.value)`</strong></p>
<p>No significant autocorrelation detected. The Q–Q plot also shows some departures from normality.</p>
</div>

</div>

::: {.slide11-caution}
**Key finding:** Neither Ljung–Box test detected significant autocorrelation. However, the **small sample and departures from normality** mean that the **2030 prediction intervals should be interpreted cautiously**.
:::

::: {.slide11-note}
**Notes:** Diagnostics use residuals from the full-history linear models. Non-significant tests do not prove residual independence. Prediction intervals remain conditional on model assumptions. **Methods:** [@HyndmanAthanasopoulos2021]. **Results:** Project model diagnostics.
:::

:::

```{r}
# -------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Validate the forecast data
```


::: {.slide13}

::: {.slide13-intro}
**Scenario approach:** GPU projections compare alternative growth assumptions using only **five annual observations (2022 - 2026)**. Research-field scenarios apply historical **allocation shares** to the selected 2030 national HPC demand projection.
:::

:::: {.slide13-panels}

::: {.slide13-panel}

::: {.slide13-title}
GPU: Exploratory 2030 scenarios
:::

::: {.slide13-subtitle}
Million GPU-hours under alternative forecasting assumptions
:::

::: {.slide13-visual}

::: {.slide13-chart}

```{r}
#| label: slide13-gpu-chart
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(
  gpu_2030,
  aes(
    x = scenario,
    y = value,
    fill = reference
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.62
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = sprintf("%.2f", value)
    ),
    hjust = -0.18,
    size = 4.1,
    fontface = "bold",
    colour = "#17324D"
  ) +
  coord_flip(
    clip = "off"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Benchmark" = "#006DAE",
      "Alternative" = "#A7CBE1"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 4.25),
    breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4),
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0, 0)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 11
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(
      size = 10,
      colour = "#17324D"
    ),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      size = 10,
      colour = "#555"
    ),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.margin = margin(
      5, 18, 5, 5
    )
  )
```

:::

:::

::: {.slide13-explanation}
The **naïve benchmark** had the lowest one-step-ahead RMSE, but evaluation covered only **two years**.

Alternative assumptions produce **2.25 - 3.68 million GPU-hours in 2030**. This range illustrates **model sensitivity**, not a statistical prediction interval.
:::

:::

::: {.slide13-panel}

::: {.slide13-title}
Research-field allocation-share scenarios
:::

::: {.slide13-subtitle}
Illustrative distribution of projected 2030 national demand using historical allocation shares
:::

::: {.slide13-visual}

<div class="slide13-method">

<p>
<strong>Calculation:</strong>
2030 national HPC demand × recent FoR allocation share
</p>

<p>
<strong>Example:</strong>
2,500,000 kSU × 33.28% =
<strong>832,000 kSU</strong>
(Engineering &amp; Technology)
</p>

</div>

::: {.slide13-table}

| Research field | 2014–20 | 2021–26 | 2030 kSU* |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Engineering & Technology | 16.24% | 33.28% | 832,000 |
| Earth & Environmental Sciences | 30.38% | 13.36% | 334,000 |
| Physical Sciences | 16.26% | 21.11% | 527,750 |
| Chemical Sciences | 18.28% | 17.02% | 425,500 |

:::

:::

::: {.slide13-explanation}
The **2021 - 2026 shares** provide the recent reference scenario; 2014 - 2020 shows historical differences, with comparisons affected by the **ANZSRC classification change**.

These are **conditional illustrative allocations**, not independent forecasts of field-level researcher demand.
:::

:::

::::

::: {.slide13-bottom}
**Planning implication:** These results provide a transparent starting point for national HPC planning, but GPU projections remain sensitive to modelling assumptions and research-field estimates depend on historical allocation patterns. More detailed demand and usage data would support more reliable, field-specific forecasts.
:::

::: {.slide13-note}
**Notes:** GPU scenarios are not statistical prediction intervals. The naïve benchmark holds estimated 2026 GPU demand constant. *2030 FoR values apply 2021 - 2026 allocation shares to the rounded 2.50 million kSU national HPC projection; only four research fields are shown. Historical FoR comparisons span the ANZSRC 2008/2020 classification change. Allocation shares are not direct measures of researcher demand.
:::

::: {.slide13-source}
**Source:** Project scenario forecasting analysis, Chapter 10.
:::

:::

<div class="slide14">

<div class="slide14-headline">
This project provides a reproducible starting point for national HPC demand forecasting. Further collaboration with NCI and Pawsey to harmonise demand data would strengthen future planning and investment decisions.
</div>

<div class="slide14-grid">

<div class="slide14-colhead">
What the analysis found
</div>

<div class="slide14-colhead">
What the Academy can do next
</div>

</div>

<!-- Finding 1: Overall HPC -->

<div class="slide14-pair">

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>Overall HPC: 2.50 million kSU by 2030</strong>
<p>
Selected linear projection; 95% prediction interval:
<b>1.98 - 3.03 million kSU</b>.
</p>
</div>

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>Establish a national planning baseline</strong>
<p>
Use the projection and its uncertainty range as an
initial planning scenario, not a fixed infrastructure
capacity target.
</p>
</div>

</div>

<!-- Finding 2: CPU -->

<div class="slide14-pair">

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>CPU: 1.37 billion core-hours by 2030</strong>
<p>
Selected linear projection; 95% prediction interval:
<b>0.97 - 1.77 billion core-hours</b>.
</p>
</div>

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>Plan CPU requirements separately</strong>
<p>
Use CPU core-hours alongside overall HPC service units,
recognising differences in resource accounting
and comparability.
</p>
</div>

</div>

<!-- Finding 3: GPU -->

<div class="slide14-pair">

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>GPU: Longer-term forecasts remain uncertain</strong>
<p>
Only five annual observations (2022 - 2026);
the naïve model achieved the lowest RMSE
across just two one-step-ahead evaluations.
</p>
</div>

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>Retain GPU scenarios, not a single target</strong>
<p>
Use the naïve benchmark for comparison
and refine projections as longer, more detailed
GPU demand and usage records become available.
</p>
</div>

</div>

<!-- Finding 4: Fields of Research -->

<div class="slide14-pair">

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>FoR: Engineering leads recent allocations</strong>
<p>
Engineering &amp; Technology accounts for
<b>33.28%</b> and Physical Sciences for
<b>21.11%</b> of 2021 - 2026 allocation shares.
</p>
</div>

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>Develop research-field demand evidence</strong>
<p>
Use historical allocation shares for illustrative
scenarios while working towards consistent,
directly observed field-level demand data.
</p>
</div>

</div>

<!-- Finding 5: Data comparability -->

<div class="slide14-pair">

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>Data comparability is a key challenge</strong>
<p>
Historical NCI and Pawsey data differ in reporting
scope, resource units and accounting conventions,
requiring transparent harmonisation assumptions.
</p>
</div>

<div class="slide14-cell">
<strong>Build a consistent national demand dataset</strong>
<p>
Standardise units and definitions; distinguish
requests, allocations and fulfilment; and document
conversion rules and data provenance.
</p>
</div>

</div>

<div class="slide14-bottom">
<p>
<strong>Recommended next step:</strong>
The Academy can build on this project's
data-integration workflow, forecasting models and
scenario framework as a <b>proof of concept</b>,
collaborating with NCI and Pawsey to refine national
HPC demand estimates as more detailed data become available.
</p>
</div>

<div class="slide14-note">
<p>
<strong>Notes:</strong>
HPC and CPU projections use selected linear models including 2026;
95% prediction intervals are conditional on model assumptions.
GPU scenarios are exploratory.
FoR percentages represent historical allocation shares,
not directly observed demand.
Overall HPC service units and CPU core-hours are different
accounting measures.
<strong>Source:</strong>
Project data integration, standardisation and forecasting analyses,
Chapters 03 - 10.
</p>
</div>

</div>

<div class="slide4-wrap">

<div class="slide4-heading">
Three Steps to Make Historical Data Comparable
</div>

<div class="slide4-steps">

<div class="slide4-step">
<div class="slide4-step-title">Step 1 | Identify</div>
Identify the computing system and its reporting units: kSU, CPU core-hours or GPU-hours.
</div>

<div class="slide4-step">
<div class="slide4-step-title">Step 2 | Convert</div>
Use conversion factors for each system to calculate CPU core-hours or GPU-hours.
</div>

<div class="slide4-step">
<div class="slide4-step-title">Step 3 | Combine</div>
Combine compatible data by year, keeping CPU and GPU separate.
</div>

</div>

<div class="slide4-heading">
System-Specific Conversion Rules
</div>

<table class="slide4-table">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Supercomputer</th>
<th>Conversion from kSU</th>
<th>Output</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Raijin CPU*</td>
<td>kSU × 1,000 ÷ 1</td>
<td>CPU core-hours</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Gadi CPU</td>
<td>kSU × 1,000 ÷ 2</td>
<td>CPU core-hours</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Setonix CPU</td>
<td>kSU × 1,000 ÷ 1</td>
<td>CPU core-hours</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Setonix GPU</td>
<td>kSU × 1,000 ÷ 128</td>
<td>GPU-hours</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div style="font-size: 0.7em; color: #666; margin-top: 5px;">
*Raijin uses an assumed historical conversion factor.
These are the rules used in this project; they may vary by system and reporting year.
</div>

<div class="slide4-caution">
<strong>Important:</strong> Service units (kSU) are system-specific. Some historical conversions rely on assumptions, so comparisons across years require care.
</div>

<div class="slide4-sources">
Sources: NCMAS information for applicants
[@NCMAS2014Info; @NCMAS2020Info; @NCMAS2023Info; @NCMAS2026Info].
Conversion factors: project year-by-year conversion methodology.
</div>
